attempts.entry_title: Movement encoding across brain areas (Wang et al. 2025) on the Mesoscale Activity Map
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings could not be tested in this data. How much movement explains activity across and within brain areas, whether neurons lead or follow movement, and decoding choice from video all need the video or its autoencoder embedding, which the cited dataset version lacks. Of the 106 sessions the paper used, 72 have no video in any version. The data do hold the stated scale of neurons and structures, and the mouse-specific pattern of choice decoding from jaw and nose markers appears, though weaker than reported. The paper does not describe its choice decoder, and the one used here was weaker, which may explain the gap.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Wang, Kurgyis, Chen et al. (2025) on dandiset 000363, which holds 174 Neuropixels sessions of 28 mice in a delayed-response task, with three DeepLabCut markers from the side camera. The version the paper cites has no video, the later version has it for only 34 of the paper's 106 sessions, and the paper's autoencoder embedding and end-to-end networks cannot be computed here, so only the unit counts and the clustering of marker-based choice decoding by mouse are tested; the other claims are blocked.

outcomes.statement: The analysis covers more than 50,000 neurons recorded in more than a dozen cortical and subcortical structures, simultaneously with high-speed video of orofacial movements.
outcomes.source: Main text, Introduction, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: we analyzed recordings of more than 50,000 neurons, recorded in more than a dozen cortical and subcortical structures, simultaneously with high-speed video of orofacial movements
outcomes.notes: Over the 174 sessions, all with video markers, 272,227 units; unit_quality good 154,948 and classification good 69,453. With the 2 Hz filter on avg_firing_rate, 88,647 and 46,658, so after the filter the count is above 50,000 under unit_quality and below it under classification; the criterion holds when either count exceeds 50,000, and the count before the filter does under both. Only units with classification good carry a CCF annotation: the 200,922 units with an empty anno_name are exactly the classification unlabelled ones, so 92,769 of the 154,948 unit_quality good units have no CCF location and 62,179 have one. Counted without nesting, each annotated unit once in its major Allen division with isocortex split into ALM and other isocortex, the units fall in 13 structures (ALM, other isocortex, olfactory areas, hippocampal formation, cortical subplate, striatum, pallidum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, medulla, cerebellum), each with at least 100 units, under both labels, with or without the 2 Hz filter, and over the 174 sessions or the authors' 106. That is more than 12 by one, and it rests on counting ALM and other isocortex apart, as the criterion's list of areas does; without the split it would be 12. ALM here is the isocortex units on probes targeted to ALM, so it may include neighbouring motor cortex; the margin is narrow. About 40 units are in names the structure tree lacks (parts of the dorsal lateral geniculate complex, in the thalamus), which adds no structure. The 16 areas of area2anno.json nest (Thalamus holds VM, VAL and MD; Midbrain holds SC, MRN, SNr and PPN); their top-level areas with ALM give 10, so they are not the count. Over the authors' 106 sessions, 90,324 unit_quality good and 42,259 classification good units (28,606 above 2 Hz). measured gives the unit_quality good count and the number of structures.
deviations: The 2 Hz filter uses the dataset's whole-session avg_firing_rate, not the rate over the included trials (Methods, Prediction of neural activity, 'Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were excluded'); the count before the filter already decides the claim.

The paper names no quality label; both of the dataset's (unit_quality and classification) are reported, as the criterion allows. Units with unit_quality good but no CCF annotation count towards the neuron count and not towards any structure.

Structures are the twelve major divisions of the Allen CCF, read from the authors' structure tree in their deposit (mousebrainontology_2.csv and mousebrainontology_heirarchy_cortexMaskExclusions21_sc.xlsx), with isocortex split into ALM (units on probes targeted to ALM, as the code's get_single_area_inds) and other isocortex, the level of the areas the criterion lists; each unit is counted once. A layer name missing from the tree takes the path of its area.

deviations: The marker decoder is not described in the paper and its code is not public; the claims file's readings (a) five-frame window, 10 features, and (b) single frame, 2 features, were run with L2 logistic regression, the penalty chosen by inner fivefold cross-validation from C in 0.01 to 100 (the grid of the paper's code, functions_for_r2.calculate_auc). Correct trials only with 20-fold stratified cross-validation (Methods, Trial selection and cross-validation). The paper does not say how the AUC at a time bin is formed from the folds. The main reading averages the test-fold AUCs, as the Methods do for the other cross-validated measures (Methods, 'Defining choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated neurons using video-based choice decoder', 'The final AUC for each neuron is the average of the test AUC across all test-folds'; 'Epoch-averaged explained variance', 'After this, the folds were averaged'); one AUC over the pooled out-of-fold decision values is a variant. Both give the same outcome.

The AUC is computed every 20th frame (68 ms) from -1.2 s to the go cue and averaged over the 17 bins, an assumption made to keep the run within time (the paper decodes each time bin); a mean over bins changes by noise only. The trimmed epoch (-1.05 to -0.15 s) is a variant.

Marker outliers above five standard deviations of the frame-to-frame velocity are replaced by linear interpolation (Methods, 'We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on velocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames'). No velocity is taken across the gap between two trial videos; a frame is flagged when the velocity into it is an outlier, so a single bad frame also flags the next one (median 8.7 frames per 10,000 imputed).

The main set is the 106 sessions the paper used, named in the authors' Fig. 6 and 7 file and matched by link-authors-deposit; the sessions that pass the clock check and all decoded sessions are variants and give the same outcome. Seven sessions fail the clock check (see findings), none of them among the 106. Since the main set comes from the authors' deposit, the claim's data field is set to with_labels in the claims file and it depends on link-authors-deposit.

Two sessions are not decoded, SC032_121719 (8 correct left trials) and SC066_041321 (4 correct trials with marker frames over the delay epoch, as markers exist for 7 trial videos only); neither is among the authors' 106.

For the 34 that have it, reading the side view alone takes more than an hour a session (1.4 h at the rate of the final run, 47 h for the 34; the timed rate varies from run to run) before any network is trained on four CPUs, so they are also too large to compute here. The authors' per-frame embeddings are not in their Zenodo deposit (session_latents.pkl holds 16 images of 120 by 112 pixels for each of the 106 sessions), and the Google Drive folder the code's README links has no DOI or fixed version, so the protocol does not allow its use (author step 1.4). The deposit's per-neuron explained variances and choice AUCs are the paper's own results, not data, and are not used. This claim trains a shared encoder on 40 sessions' video and compares it with the session-specific autoencoders and the markers.

findings.statement: In five sessions, sub-440959 (SC011) on 2019-02-24, 2019-02-25 and 2019-02-26 and sub-442571 (SC022) on 2019-02-27 and 2019-02-28, the DeepLabCut marker timestamps advance 3.4 ms per frame but the video frames are 6.8 ms apart. As deposited, the tongue is visible at 6 to 13% of the lick events, and no shift of the lick times within 1 s brings this above 0.49; stretching each trial's marker timestamps by 2 from its first frame puts the tongue at 99.9 to 100% of the licks. Their trial videos hold 934 to 946 frames (median per session), against 1864 to 1886 in the other eight sessions of the same two mice, although the trials last as long (median 4.83 to 4.90 s in all 13) and each video starts at its trial's start; the median over all sessions is 1904. The video in the later version holds the same frame counts and carries no timing (a starting time with a rate of 1.0, no timestamps), so the 6.8 ms spacing is inferred from the frame counts and the licks, not read from the video. The markers of these sessions are on a time base half as long as the trial table's, and nothing in the files shows it; any analysis of movement around task events in them comes out wrong.
findings.checked: The printed outputs show it. Cell 8: the tongue-after-go-cue contrast is negative in 5 sessions. Cell 10: as deposited, the tongue is visible at 0.063 to 0.132 of lick events; the best fraction at any shift within 1 s is 0.484; stretching the timestamps by 2 gives 0.999 to 1.0. These sessions have 934 to 946 frames per trial video, against a median of 1904. Caveat: 6.8 ms apart is inferred from the x2 stretch, not measured; these sessions have video in 0.231012.2129 (cell 14), which could confirm it directly. The rating is right: signals on different clocks, the marker time base half as long as the trial table's, and nothing in the files labels it. The short videos are visible in the data but do not reveal the timing error. Any marker-to-event analysis of these sessions would come out wrong, although none of them is in the authors' 106.

findings.statement: In sub-455219 on 2019-08-07 (SC026_080719) the tongue is visible at 60% of lick events: 214 trial videos match the licks and 117 do not, and the session has 539 trial videos for 630 trials, so some videos are probably attached to the wrong trials. The cause was not established.

Marker frames are missing for whole trials in two sessions: sub-484676 on 2021-04-13 (SC066_041321) has markers for 7 trial videos (49 s) of 550 trials, and sub-484674 on 2021-05-05 (SC065_050521) lacks them for 140 of its 354 correct trials. The files do not say so.

The version the paper cites (0.230822.0128) holds no video and no autoencoder embedding, the input of most of the paper's analyses. The later version 0.231012.2129 (65.7 TB) adds the raw electrophysiology to 169 files and the raw video to 71 of them (renamed +image, 28.9 TB), from 16 of the 28 mice; 34 of the 106 sessions the paper used for Figs. 6 and 7 have video and 72 have none in any version. Units, trials and markers of four sessions drawn at random are identical in both versions. The authors' per-frame embeddings are in no pinned deposit.

The marker timestamps step by exactly 3.4 ms within a trial (99.9% of intervals to the microsecond), a frame rate of 294 Hz, where the paper states 300 Hz; they look written from a nominal rate, not measured.

Units carry two quality labels, unit_quality (good or multi, no description) and classification (good or unlabelled, 1,852 NaN), and only units with classification good have a CCF annotation (anno_name is empty for all 200,922 unlabelled units), so 92,769 of the 154,948 unit_quality good units have no location. Which label the paper's 50,000 neurons use is not said.

verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebook of the first run with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier queried the archive's asset lists and metadata for both versions, and tested decode_auc_fast, marker_epoch and clean_marker on synthetic inputs (its points 9: decode_auc_fast agrees with sklearn to within 0.015 AUC, marker_epoch aligns bins, no train/test leakage; no change needed). It found no misreading of the paper in the claims file for the tested claims, so no question was added for a reader. Point 7 (the docstring said every 10th frame where STRIDE is 20): corrected, and the subsampling is now stated as an assumption. Point 8 (velocity across trial videos, a bad frame flagging the next): velocity is no longer taken across the gap between trial videos; the second flag is kept and stated. Point 10: the link claim is described as written into the claims file by this attempt, and the later version's growth is attributed to the raw electrophysiology in 169 files and the video in 71. Its request to list the Zenodo deposit is met: the notebook prints every member and its size and what session_latents.pkl holds. Report in transcripts/wang-2025/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: Neuron count holds, 154,948 units with unit_quality good, 88,647 of them above 2 Hz; 69,453 carry a CCF annotation (classification good). The structure count does not hold as computed: 17 areas counts nested structures twice (superior colliculus, MRN and SNr inside midbrain; VM, VAL and MD inside thalamus); without the nesting the listed groups give about 10, not more than 12. About 132 dataset annotations fall outside the map and were never grouped (point 1). The 92,769 unit_quality good units have no CCF location and the notebook does not point this out (point 2).

verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook of the run after round 1, with its conclusions and summary, the helper module, the attempt record and the claims file, with the paper. It agreed with all 30 outcomes and found the assumptions they rest on stated and reasonable (session AUC as the mean of the test-fold AUCs, 68 ms bins, ALM split from other isocortex by probe target, the 2 Hz filter on avg_firing_rate). It reported no place where the claims file misreads the paper, so no question was added for a reader. Of the sentences it found the numbers do not support, the read rate in the blocked notes and the 167 sessions of the fig6e variant are corrected (see those claims), and finding 7, which said the Methods give 105 and 106 sessions where the 105 is in the Results (Fig. 2c to e), now says so. It found round-1 points 1 to 10 and C resolved. On finding 2 (SC026_080719, major) it would consider critical if the misassignment of videos to trials were confirmed, and called major defensible since the cause is not established and the count mismatch is visible in the files; it stays major, as testing the misassignment is a new analysis that would not fit in the notebook's 60-minute limit (the re-run took 59.8 minutes). After the round the entry was re-run with one added cell (cell 11, the frame spacing of the flagged sessions without the licks) and six workers in place of four for reading the sessions; every printed number other than the timed video read rate is unchanged. Report in transcripts/wang-2025/verifier-2-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: The dataset holds 174 sessions of 28 mice; the authors' Fig. 6 and 7 file names 106 sessions of 21 mice, and seven mice (SC011, SC013, SC015, SC016, SC017, SC022, SC023) have none. The Methods say 28 mice, and the Results give 105 sessions for Fig. 2c-e and 106 for Fig. 6, without saying which sessions were used or why the others were left out.

Question for the authors. The choice decoder of Fig. 6 (from the embedding and from single markers) is not described in the Methods and its code is in neither public repository. Which classifier, features (single frame or the five-frame window), penalty selection and time resolution were used, and was the AUC of a time bin averaged over test folds or computed over pooled out-of-fold predictions? This attempt used L2 logistic regression with a nested choice of penalty on one or five frames of one marker, an AUC per 68 ms bin averaged over the delay epoch; on the authors' 106 sessions the Calinski-Harabasz score of Fig. 6e is 6.4 to 6.8 with test-fold AUCs averaged and 7.6 to 7.9 with pooled AUCs, against the paper's 12.57, and the best single marker gives a response-epoch AUC of 0.75 against the paper's 0.88.

entries.description: Tests the findings of Wang, Kurgyis, Chen et al. (2025) on dandiset 000363, which holds 174 Neuropixels sessions of 28 mice in a delayed-response task, with three DeepLabCut markers from the side camera. The version the paper cites has no video, the later version has it for only 34 of the paper's 106 sessions, and the paper's autoencoder embedding and end-to-end networks cannot be computed here, so only the unit counts and the clustering of marker-based choice decoding by mouse are tested; the other claims are blocked.
